nameStory: Glaucous honeysuckle gets its name from its distinctive blue-green leaves that have a waxy, frosted appearance called 'glaucous' — the same coating you see on fresh blueberries. The honeysuckle part comes from the sweet nectar in its tubular flowers, which people have long enjoyed sipping (though the berries of most honeysuckles shouldn't be eaten).
description: Glaucous honeysuckle is a native climbing vine that twines its way up trees and shrubs, reaching 6-12 feet in height. Its most striking feature is the blue-green, waxy coating on its leaves that gives them a frosted appearance. The vine produces pairs of yellow to orange tubular flowers followed by bright red berries, and it's one of our native honeysuckles that wildlife actually benefit from, unlike many of the invasive honeysuckle species.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Distinctive blue-green leaves with a waxy, frosted coating that feels smooth and slightly thick to the touch. The uppermost pairs of leaves are fused together around the stem, forming cup-like discs.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Yellow to orange tubular flowers appear in pairs at the ends of branches, sitting right in the center of those fused upper leaves like flowers in a natural vase.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: A twining vine that spirals clockwise around supports, with stems that feel relatively smooth and flexible when young but become woody with age.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Bright red berries appear in pairs where the flowers were, sitting prominently in the cup formed by the fused leaves.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Older stems develop light brown bark that peels in thin, papery strips, revealing lighter wood underneath.

habitat: Look for glaucous honeysuckle in rocky or sandy soils in open woodlands, forest edges, and clearings throughout New England. It particularly favors areas with some disturbance like old logging sites or woodland borders, often climbing up small trees and shrubs in partially sunny locations.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge with their characteristic blue-green waxy coating, and you can see the developing flower buds at branch tips.
seasonality.summer: Yellow to orange flowers bloom in early to mid-summer, followed by the development of bright red berries later in the season.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn yellowish before dropping, and bright red berries are most prominent and easiest to spot against the changing foliage.
seasonality.winter: Leafless vines show their twining growth pattern and peeling bark, with some dried berry remnants occasionally persisting.

funFact: The fused upper leaves of glaucous honeysuckle actually collect dew and rainwater, creating tiny natural bird baths that provide drinking water for insects and small birds — it's like the plant designs its own wildlife watering station!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with invasive honeysuckles like Japanese or Morrow's honeysuckle, but those lack the distinctive waxy blue-green coating and fused upper leaves. Remember: 'If it's glaucous and the leaves make cups, it's our native one!'
contextualKnowledge: This is one of the 'good' honeysuckles — unlike the invasive Asian species that dominate many New England areas, glaucous honeysuckle is native and provides genuine benefit to local wildlife. Many people are surprised to learn that not all honeysuckles are invasive problems.
compareHints: Among New England's honeysuckles, glaucous honeysuckle is the only climbing species with that distinctive waxy blue-green leaf coating and cup-forming fused upper leaves. The fly honeysuckles in our region are upright shrubs rather than vines, while other climbing honeysuckles like Japanese honeysuckle have green leaves without the waxy coating and different leaf arrangements.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the invasive Japanese, Morrow's, and Tatarian honeysuckles that dominate many New England areas, American fly-honeysuckle has distinctively paired berries and a much more restrained growth habit.
Japanese honeysuckle is unique among New England honeysuckles for its white-to-yellow color change and semi-evergreen leaves.
Unlike native fly honeysuckles which have flowers in clusters and blue or black berries, Morrow's honeysuckle has flowers and berries strictly in pairs with red fruit.
Unlike native American fly-honeysuckle which stays small and has paired flowers on long stalks, Amur honeysuckle grows into a large shrub with flowers sitting directly on the branches.
Among New England honeysuckles, coral honeysuckle is the only one with scentless, coral-red tubular flowers and that distinctive leaf-fusion around the stem.
Unlike our native fly honeysuckles which have flowers in clusters and blue or black berries, Tatarian honeysuckle always has paired flowers and red berries.
Mountain fly-honeysuckle differs from American fly honeysuckle by having much fuzzier leaves and preferring higher elevation habitats.
Among New England's honeysuckles, the dense coating of soft hairs immediately separates this species from smooth-leaved Japanese honeysuckle or the only slightly hairy American fly honeysuckle.
Fly honeysuckle stands out from other honeysuckles in New England by its paired red berries and shrubby growth habit - most others either climb like vines or have different colored berries.
Unlike the vigorous vining Japanese honeysuckle, winter honeysuckle is a well-behaved shrub that doesn't climb.
Unlike the more common American fly honeysuckle which prefers drier woods, swamp fly honeysuckle demands wet feet and boggy conditions.

Unlike the ubiquitous Japanese honeysuckle which blooms white to yellow and has simple opposite leaves, common honeysuckle has those distinctive fused upper leaves and more intensely fragrant flowers.
While New England has many honeysuckle species, perfoliate honeysuckle is the only one with fused upper leaves that the stem appears to grow through.
Unlike the invasive Asian honeysuckles that plague New England (Japanese, Morrow's, Amur), twinberry honeysuckle doesn't spread aggressively and has the unique twin-berry-in-red-bracts feature.
Unlike the aggressive Japanese honeysuckle that stays white then turns yellow, grape honeysuckle flowers age to pink.
Unlike its weedy relatives like Japanese honeysuckle (which climbs) or Morrow's honeysuckle (which has red berries), sweetberry honeysuckle stays compact and produces edible blue fruit.
